references.text: God created light and separated it from darkness – this is the immediate context for the naming of day and night in verse 5.
On the fourth day, God placed lights in the sky to separate day from night, as a continuation of the separation between light and darkness on day one.
Day and night belong to God; He has established both light and the sun – a praise of God's dominion over day and night, which He named in creation.
God causes it to become dark, and it becomes night – an expression of God's ongoing governance of the alternation between day and night that He established in creation.
The Lord who forms light and creates darkness – a direct parallel to God's creation and naming of day (light) and night (darkness) in Genesis 1:5.
Paul draws a parallel between God, who let light shine out of darkness at creation, and the spiritual light of the gospel.
By faith we understand that the world was created by God's word, pointing back to God's creative and ordering acts in the creation account.
The fixed formula for the end of each creation day confirms the rhythmic order of the creation narrative.
The creation of the sun and moon to regulate the days and nights first named in 1:5.
Confirmation that the separation of light and darkness, which occurred on day one, is part of God's good work of creation.
A prophetic contrast where the original separation of day and night is abolished in a future, divine unity.
Contrast between God's firm separation of light and darkness and humanity's attempt to distort this order.
Explanation of the purpose of the separation of day and night introduced on the first day.
The fixed formula for the end of each creation day confirms the rhythmic order of the creation narrative.
Confirmation of God's sovereign control over the time periods He Himself separated and named.
